summary: Describes UDP-Lite, a variant of UDP that lets an application say how much of each packet the checksum must cover. Packets with damage outside that area can still be delivered, which suits audio and video that tolerate some bit errors, especially on noisy links. With full coverage it behaves like UDP.

eli5.summary: Normally a package with any scratch is thrown away. UDP-Lite lets you say a small scratch is okay, so a mostly fine song or video still arrives.

subtitle: UDP with a flexible checksum, so damaged audio or video can still reach the application.

tldr.problem: UDP checksums cover the whole packet or nothing at all, so on error-prone links a packet with a few damaged payload bits is discarded even when a voice or video codec could have coped with it.
tldr.mechanism: UDP-Lite replaces the UDP Length field with a Checksum Coverage field. The checksum protects only the first part of the packet (always including the header), and errors after that point do not cause the packet to be discarded.
tldr.outcome: Applications that want partial protection get it, while full coverage makes UDP-Lite semantically identical to UDP. It has its own IP protocol number, 136. RFC 3828 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6335.

today: RFC 3828 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6335. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Damaged Data Can Be Useful
sections.content:
RFC 3828 starts from three observations. First, some applications benefit from receiving damaged data rather than nothing. The RFC names voice and video codecs such as the AMR speech codec, the Internet Low Bit Rate Codec, and error resilient H.263+, H.264 and MPEG-4, which may cope better with errors in the payload than with the loss of whole packets.

Second, all links that carry IP should use a strong link layer integrity check, and that MUST be used by default. When the link supports it, certain traffic such as UDP-Lite may be allowed to forward partially damaged IP packets on request. Several radio technologies support this behavior.

Third, the layers above the link should not get in the way. IP is fine, because the IPv4 header checksum does not cover the payload. UDP is the best available transport, but in IPv4 its checksum covers either the entire packet or nothing, and in IPv6 the UDP checksum is mandatory and must not be disabled.
sections.eli5: Imagine a song on a scratched CD. If one tiny scratch makes the player throw the whole song away, that is silly. Some songs sound fine with a small scratch.

sections.title: The UDP-Lite Header and Its Fields
sections.content:
The header looks like the UDP header, with one change: the Length field is replaced by Checksum Coverage. This works because the packet length can be obtained from the IP module, the same way TCP does it. The header has four 16-bit fields: Source Port, Destination Port, Checksum Coverage and Checksum, followed by the payload.

Ports are defined as in UDP, and UDP-Lite uses the same port number values assigned by IANA for UDP.

Checksum Coverage is the number of octets, counted from the first octet of the UDP-Lite header, that the checksum covers. The header MUST always be covered. A value of zero means the entire packet is covered. Otherwise the value MUST be at least 8, and a packet with a coverage of 1 to 7 MUST be discarded by the receiver, as MUST a packet whose coverage is greater than the IP length.
sections.eli5: The label on the package has a new box that says how much of the package you promise to check for damage. The label itself is always checked.

sections.title: How the Checksum Is Computed
sections.content:
The Checksum field is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of three things: a pseudo-header collected from the IP header, the number of octets given by Checksum Coverage (starting at the first octet of the UDP-Lite header), and a virtual zero octet of padding if needed to make a multiple of two octets. Before computing, the checksum field MUST be set to zero. If the result is 0, it is transmitted as all ones.

Because the transmitted checksum MUST NOT be all zeroes, an application that wants no protection for the payload should use a Checksum Coverage of 8. This still differs from UDP over IPv4 with no checksum, because the minimal UDP-Lite checksum always covers the header, including the Checksum Coverage field.

The pseudo-header is the same idea as in UDP, with one difference: its Length value is not taken from the UDP-Lite header. It comes from the IP module, as for TCP, and includes the UDP-Lite header and all following octets of the IP payload.
sections.eli5: The checksum is a quick math score of the part you chose to protect. The receiver redoes the math, and if the scores differ, the package is thrown away.

sections.title: Application and IP Interfaces
sections.content:
The application interface should allow the same operations as UDP, plus a way for the sender to pass in the Checksum Coverage value. There should also be a way to pass the coverage value to the receiving application, or at least let the receiver block delivery of packets with coverage below a value it chooses.

It is RECOMMENDED that the default mimic UDP: coverage matching the whole packet. Applications that treat part of the payload as insensitive to bit errors, for example error tolerant codecs using RTP, should ask for that with an explicit system call on the sender side, and receivers wanting partly covered payloads should also ask explicitly. Applications should not assume the data beyond the coverage point is correct, and should add their own validity checks if needed.

On the IP side, the IP module must provide the pseudo-header, and the sender IP module MUST NOT pad the IP payload with extra octets, because the UDP-Lite payload length seen by the receiver depends on the IP payload length. For Jumbograms, the checksum can cover either the entire payload (coverage zero) or at most the initial 65535 octets.
sections.eli5: By default the program checks everything, like UDP. Only a program that asks can say that the end of the package may be a bit scratched.

sections.title: Lower Layers and Compatibility with UDP
sections.content:
A link that supports partial error detection MAY use the Checksum Coverage field as a hint of where errors need not be detected. Lower layers MUST still use a strong error detection mechanism for the sensitive part, which runs from the first octet of the IP header to the last octet named by the coverage, and discard packets damaged there. Links without suitable partial detection MUST check the whole packet and discard damaged ones, so the packet is treated exactly like UDP. The RFC notes that UDP-Lite only makes a difference to an application if link layers also implement partial error detection over error-prone links.

UDP-Lite has its own IP protocol identifier, 136 (UDPLite). A host that does not know UDP-Lite will generally return an ICMP Protocol Unreachable or an ICMPv6 Payload Type Unknown error, which is the main benefit of a separate identifier. If the identifier were shared with UDP, a UDP receiver would silently discard a partially covered UDP-Lite packet because the pseudo-header would not match and the checksum would fail, with neither application told.
sections.eli5: The postal workers only get to skip checking the scratched part if they know how. Otherwise they check everything. UDP-Lite also has its own stamp, so a mailbox that does not understand it can say so.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main security impact is how UDP-Lite interacts with authentication and encryption. With partial coverage, the insensitive part may change in transit, which conflicts with authentication that succeeds only if the packet is unchanged. Unless authentication that works only on the sensitive part is developed and used, authentication will fail for UDP-Lite packets with a damaged insensitive part.

The IPsec integrity check (ESP or AH) applies to at least the entire IP payload, so corruption of any protected bit leads to the packet being discarded. With ESP payload encryption, a link cannot see the transport protocol, so it MUST provide a standard integrity check over the whole packet, and UDP-Lite provides no benefit.

Encryption transforms that spread errors usually make a slightly damaged packet useless. Some transforms and stream ciphers do not propagate errors, but omitting an integrity check can in some circumstances compromise confidentiality, and stream ciphers pose their own challenges, such as an attacker causing predictable changes to the plaintext.
sections.eli5: A tamper seal breaks if anything changes. If you allow some scratching, the seal cannot tell scratches from tampering, so seals and UDP-Lite do not mix well.

fields.name: Checksum Coverage
fields.desc: Octets covered by the checksum, from the first header octet. 0 means the whole packet; otherwise at least 8.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum over a pseudo-header and the covered octets.
